```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r}
library(seqbench)
```

The guarantee of `seqbench` rests on four assumptions, recorded in every report:

* **A1**: instances are independent draws from the population of interest, run in an order
  that does not depend on their losses;
* **A2**: the number and values of the seeds of an instance are fixed without looking at any
  of its losses;
* **A3**: both losses lie within the declared bounds;
* **A4**: an instance whose losses were seen is never reused.

This vignette explains why the *instance*, not the evaluation, is the sequential unit, and
what the package refuses to do.

## Seeds are a cluster

Runs of a randomised algorithm on the same instance with different seeds are not independent
replications of the comparison. They share the instance, and the instance usually matters
more than the seed. `seqbench` therefore averages the seeds of an instance into a single
observation:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
make <- function(n, m, mu = 0.03, w = 0.08) {
  inst <- rep(seq_len(n), each = m)
  v <- runif(n, -w, w)[inst]                   # instance-specific difference shared by its seeds
  la <- runif(n * m, 0.4, 0.6)
  data.frame(instance = inst, seed = rep(seq_len(m), n), loss_a = la,
             loss_b = la - mu - v + runif(n * m, -0.05, 0.05))
}
losses <- make(400, m = 5)
d <- comparison_design(margin = 0.01, bounds = c(0, 1), n_max = 400)
st <- suppressWarnings(update_comparison(initialize_comparison(d), losses))
head(tidy(st)[, c("t", "instance", "n_seeds", "estimate", "lower_running", "upper_running")], 3)
```

Feeding every `(instance, seed)` row as if it were its own instance is *pseudoreplication*: it
treats five correlated runs as five independent pieces of evidence, which makes the interval
too narrow. Do not do this:

```{r}
pseudo <- transform(losses, instance = seq_len(nrow(losses)), seed = 1L)   # WRONG
```

How many seeds per instance? Averaging more seeds reduces only the within-instance noise. If
running a new instance is cheap relative to running a seed, use one seed per instance and more
instances; if generating or loading an instance is expensive, a few seeds per instance can
save instances, at a cost in evaluations that the `cost` column makes visible.

## Plan all seeds before looking

The number of seeds may differ between instances, and it may depend on what was seen *in other
instances*, but never on the losses of the instance itself. Adding seeds to an instance that
"looks close" makes the observation depend on its own outcome, so it is refused:

```{r, error = TRUE}
st <- update_comparison(initialize_comparison(d), make(3, m = 2))
update_comparison(st, data.frame(instance = 2, seed = 3, loss_a = 0.5, loss_b = 0.4))
```

Give the new runs a new instance instead.

## Other refusals

The package never turns invalid input into a valid-looking result.

```{r, error = TRUE}
fresh <- initialize_comparison(d)
update_comparison(fresh, data.frame(instance = 1, loss_a = 1.2, loss_b = 0.5))   # outside bounds
update_comparison(fresh, data.frame(instance = 1, loss_a = NA, loss_b = 0.5))    # missing loss
update_comparison(fresh, data.frame(instance = c(1, 1), seed = 1,
                                    loss_a = 0.5, loss_b = 0.4))                  # duplicated pair
comparison_design(margin = 0.01, bounds = c(0, 1), paired = FALSE)                # unpaired
```

A run that failed or timed out needs a loss decided *before* it reaches the package, for
example a penalised value within the bounds. Dropping it would bias the comparison towards
the algorithm that fails more often on hard instances.

Once a comparison has reached a terminal decision it refuses further data, because the
pre-registered protocol ends there:

```{r, error = TRUE}
st <- suppressWarnings(update_comparison(initialize_comparison(d), make(400, m = 1, mu = 0.1)))
stopping_decision(st)
update_comparison(st, make(1, m = 1))
```

## What the package cannot check

Independence of instances (A1) and the absence of drift cannot be verified from the losses.
If instances arrive in time (daily operations, production traffic) or come from a fixed
benchmark library rather than a generator, think about whether "a random draw from a
population" describes them before trusting the guarantee.
